utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this summary, in the penultimate paragraph, it says the witness will say: [In English] "Human Rights Division utilised standards and commonly accepted norms found in international human rights conventions," et cetera, "including Geneva Conventions," et cetera. [Interpretation] So you speak of human rights and the Geneva Convention. My question is: Do you think that the Clinton administration, by its decision to bomb Yugoslavia, imperiled human rights?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That is totally irrelevant as far as the witness's evidence is concerned. It's totally irrelevant. She's come here to give evidence about her work and the OSCE, and you must restrict your questions to that and not ask irrelevant and political questions. No. There's no point arguing about this. Now, ask her questions about her evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness refers to the Geneva Convention, Mr. May. Does that mean that I'm not allowed to ask her about the Geneva Convention either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask relevant questions about the Geneva Convention but not irrelevant ones.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh. These are irrelevant things? All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point of your testimony, as well as of your various personal references, as far as I understood this, is saying that "As Seen, As Told" is an objective book, and the claims made therein as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make true claims, objective claims, do those who observe have to be objective observers?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that persons who are under the control of such a criminal organisation such as the KLA is, the Albanian drug Mafia, do constitute objective observers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That presupposes that the witnesses to whom the witness and her organisation spoke were under the control of the KLA. So if you want to put that question, you must ask the witness if they were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we had a witness of the other side here, an Albanian, who testified about that as well. Well, not exactly willingly, about the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And not exactly as you have put it. However, since you wish to put it, we'll put it to the witness. Ms. Mitchell, in the people that you spoke to, the various people on whose accounts you relied, Kosovo Albanians, was it your view that they were under the control of the KLA or the Mafia or drug barons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our reports are based on testimonies and interviews with thousands of individuals. Particularly during the period before the mission withdrew in Kosovo between October and March, we would have, in fact, been meeting with representatives of the KLA in order to follow up on specific allegations of human rights abuses that may have concerned them. I don't believe at any time, though, we felt that we were ever speaking to somebody that was unwilling to speak to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it well-founded to assume that interlocutors have to tell the truth, Ms. Mitchell? Can that only lead to a true and accurate assumption?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were trying to obtain when we spoke to people in Kosovo was their version of the facts as they felt they were true. We were not trying to influence them to any version of the truth that we may have believed in personally. It is always our hope that our interlocutors will tell the truth when we speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not bringing into question your goodwill to find out the truth, but do you assume that your interlocutors told you the truth?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess to make the conclusion on the truth, I would rely on the way in which the facts were handled by the organisation, and the conclusions drawn from the thousands of interviews that were conducted were done in a very careful manner. Nothing in any of the books is based on any allegation that we did not believe was well-founded and based on conclusive evidence of those allegations. So those conclusions of interviews that were conducted and that we believe to be true have been reported in these books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, for example, whether you bore in mind the following. I'm going to read out an example to you. This is an example about which the Toronto Globe and Mail wrote in September, on the 8th of September 1999, and it says there: [In English] "CBC - Canadian Broadcasting Corporation - correspondent Nancy Durham made a name for herself by venturing deep into Kosovo as a one-woman news team and bringing back moving stories about both the dead and the living. Now it turns out that one of her most touching reports about an 18-year-old girl named Rajmunda [phoen] who vowed to avenge her sister's death at Serb's hands is based on a lie. With a camera rolling --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Milosevic. You have heard us say often enough before that the views of journalists are totally irrelevant. Now, so far all you're doing is reading out some newspaper report about some totally irrelevant event. Now, if you have a relevant question for this witness, you can put it, but there's no point reading out reports which, as we've said often enough before, are not evidence. If you want to call this witness, you can call her. Now, you can ask a relevant question or we shall have to move on to another topic or close this cross-examination altogether. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, it says there precisely that when she visited after the war, she found her sister well and alive, this sister who was killed by the Serbs. And that was one of the first heartrending stories about Serb crimes. She was there and she was healthy and alive, and that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what is the question for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question for the witness is whether she bore in mind this kind of practice which was quite widespread. I can give you a great many other examples here as well. I am intentionally quoting Western sources, not Yugoslav sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which practice are you putting to the witness which you say was widespread?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Widespread, customary practice, that's what it was, to lie through their teeth about alleged atrocities that always took place in some other village, that nobody had seen, rumours were spread, et cetera, et cetera. And then, of course, propagandists of the KLA and, of course, the NATO propaganda people worked on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You put this in the form of a question as it should be put. Ms. Mitchell, in your experience in Kosovo and the experience of your team, did you find there to be a practice of lying about atrocities and then making propaganda out of them, and in particular, was there -- were there instances which you found out about people making things up which were subsequently found to be untrue? Can you assist us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, whenever you're in -- have the task of trying to document human rights violations that are going on in an armed conflict and during a massive influx and exodus of the population and then the reverse when the conflict is over, people going back, you go through great, great, great efforts to try to obtain the truth and to try to verify as much as possible the information that is being told to you by people that are often very traumatised and may have, only hours ago, escaped a very life-threatening event. So that being said, the OSCE missions that I worked in and the Human Rights Divisions that I directed during the period of the two reports during that 12-month period, established numerous protocols and procedures to ensure that the information that we were getting was being reviewed and analysed and interpreted in the most accurate of ways. And I've submitted for your review many of the procedures that we used to try to ensure that, and I'm happy to answer more questions, if that would be useful. I'm not aware of any lies being told to us about the events that we've reported on that were subsequently proved to be incorrect by physical evidence on the ground, anything like this. I think that during the course of our work, we probably did interview people often whose veracity we questioned, and as I said, we had ways of going about and checking on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be helpful if you gave us at least one example of the way in which you would verify evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the mission's withdrawal, primarily during the period of December 1998 to March 20th, there was no access for ICTY. There was no access for a lot of other international bodies that had jurisdiction over the human rights situation in Kosovo, including some of the UN committees had access getting into the area. As a result, the OSCE felt it had an added responsibility to document these violations in the absence of others being able to access the area. So when we appeared on the sites of a conflict, a killing, something of this nature, we would take statements from all of those witnesses that we could. That information was handled by very few people. It was shared only on a need-to-know basis, which was always respected by the highest levels of the mission, including the Head of Mission. That information was then kept under lock and key and provided to those officials that had whatever official jurisdiction over it, as well as follow-up visits being given with the appropriate domestic bodies, whether it was the Ministry of Justice, to discuss whatever allegations we were looking at. After the evacuation and in the preparation of the reports, the review of the information was handled differently because we weren't doing the actual follow-up work. We didn't have access to Kosovo. These were all taken out of the province. And in preparing these chapters for these reports, things were analysed geographically as well as by the specific human rights violations that were discussed by the refugee and then also according to their specific grouping, if they were a community viewed most at risk. So by analysing it in three different ways, there was three different opportunities to confirm, cross-reference with different interviews that were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you've said, one may infer that all the findings of your mission are contained in the reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's contained in these reports you're referring to are the findings of the work that was conducted primarily by the Human Rights Division within the OSCE missions. The missions had different departments that were focusing on different areas of verification that were called for under the international documents, and these reports focused on the work of the Human Rights Divisions of the three different Kosovo missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter to me in how many departments they were focused. What matters to me is whether your findings were contained in the reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission. And since they are included in the reports of the Kosovo verification mission, is it your assessment that in these reports, until you withdrew, there were no findings that would attest to human rights violations or mass expulsions or things like that? Could you corroborate that or is it perhaps that I simply haven't noticed any such thing?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I -- if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you follow that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a little clarification would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, would you make clear what you mean. The reports are about human rights violations and mass expulsions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. As far as I understood, Ms. Mitchell was head of the Department for Human Rights of the Kosovo verification mission. That is right. I imagine that is not being contested. The Kosovo Verification Mission presented its reports to the OSCE and to the member countries and to us, of course. So in these reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission, I did not find any findings related to mass violations of human rights as established by the Verification Mission. So I'm asking whether there is something else. How is it possible that they are not contained therein if that was a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can maybe clarify a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kosovo Verification Mission had many different types of reporting procedures and requirements. The mission is one of numerous field missions run by an intergovernmental political agency made up of 55 countries -- 54 countries at the time that these reports were prepared because Yugoslavia was under suspension. So there is reporting going up to the governing body of the OSCE, what's referred to as the troika, which includes the chairman in office of the existing year that we're in as well as the previous and the upcoming year. And so you would have -- we would have a series of reports going up on an ad hoc or a regular basis to the chairman in office. These would be generally out of the Head of Mission's office. Then there would be weekly reports that were distributed to the Secretariat in Vienna, and those reports would in fact have been distributed to all member states, including Yugoslavia, was given reports that were coming out of Kosovo during that period. The human rights reporting, our reporting protocols, you're getting into the internal mission structure now, and these are, with the exception of, I think, a few press releases, these are the only public reporting from the mission on the human rights situation in Kosovo. I hope that clarified things a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not answer my question. If you claim that there were mass violations of human rights during the presence of the Verification Mission, how come there are no reports of such mass violations of human rights in the reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission during their stay in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has just answered that. She's told you that these are the reports. We've got them in front of us. Mass violations, they say. So that's the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I did not understand that this book was a report that was officially submitted by the mission to the Yugoslav authorities, especially after time had gone by. But if that is your explanation, then no comment is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Ms. Mitchell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, do you know if this was issued to the Yugoslav authorities or not, the report that we've seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so, Your Honour. It was distributed. Copies of the report were distributed throughout the governmental bodies of both Serbia and Yugoslav governments, in Pristina and in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean what your book contains?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The books themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that the report of the Verification Mission, for the period up to the 20th of March, while the mission was in Kosovo, does contain all these questions that you are dealing with now in your book.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the first part of the report which covers the period October 1998 to June 1999 includes extensive documentation as we were -- as extensive as the mission was capable of doing during the build-up phases when there were other tasks calling on us, but does contain an account of significant human rights violations prior to the withdrawal of the mission; and I would say that it was our conclusion in the report that those types of events that happened prior to the mission withdrawal were repeated over and over and over again during the NATO air campaign throughout all the communities. And the examples I would refer to would be the killing of civilians in Racak, the killing of combatants of Rogovo, ambush of civilians in Rakavina, at the Vucitrn winter exercises in February where we saw a displacement of the population, burning the houses, and the Kacanik exercises where we saw displacement of the population in order to remove an UCK threat. These are the types of patterns, and these existed before the mission withdrew in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as those conflicts with the terrorists groups are concerned, you mentioned Rogovo and all the rest of it, there are separate reports about that by the Verification Mission. People were there and people were in charge of that part of the affair. And they didn't translate that as being violations of human rights but they saw it as being legitimate actions on the part of the forces of the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you really saying or trying to summarise the evidence that we've heard that the KVM regarded what happened in Racak as legitimate? If you are, that is a misrepresentation of the evidence. Now, let us move on to another topic. It seems to be pointless going around this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May -- Mr. May, I'll get to Racak in a minute. What I was referring to is Rogovo, not Racak. So it is you that is doing the distorting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us get on with the evidence and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's cut the procedure and move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What conclusions were you able to make with respect to the reasons for the exodus from Kosovo and Metohija that took place? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the accounts of the forced deportation is the one charge where I would say that the evidence that we collected was overwhelming and consistent. Of the nearly 2.800 statements that we collected from refugees in the camps in Albania and in Macedonia - and we were deployed everywhere in those areas; we were there before the refugees came - every single one of those statements described a departure from Kosovo which was less than voluntary, that it was -- people were extorted. That was one of the very common elements of their departure. Money was taken from them by the Yugoslavian and Serbian security forces. Many saw their houses being burned. They saw things being stolen from their houses by the security forces. They often arrived without identity documents, licence plates, things of this nature. Many reported that when such documents were taken from them as they were leaving Kosovo, they were told that they wouldn't need them any more that they would never be coming back. There was a lot of violence associated with the deportation, killings both as villages were being emptied and then also in the convoys. They would often fall victim to checkpoints, and you would have another round of exploitation, extortion, and killing. But our conclusion was that the forced deportation occurred over and over and over again in Kosovo. And as I said before, we had seen indications of this type of deportation first-hand in Vucitrn and in Kacanik prior to our departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And did you at all try to explain the reasons for which, for example, 100.000 citizens of Serb ethnicity, during the bombing, left Kosovo? Why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only had the opportunity to speak to very few refugees of Kosovo Serb ethnicity and this was because our mandate was limited to inside Kosovo, inside the provincial boundary at the time, and then in the camp areas in Albania and in Macedonia. So we did not have access to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rest of Yugoslavia where the majority of the Kosovo Serb refugees did in fact go and became internally displaced. Those very few Kosovo Serbs that we were able to talk to that came across the Bllace border, unlike the Kosovo Albanian refugees who said that they were fleeing because of the Yugoslav and Serbian security forces and their attack on them, because of the Serb refugees, I believe some of them did say that they were leaving because of the NATO bombing. But as I said, we spoke to just a handful compared to the thousands of Kosovo Albanians. And I do believe that that's reported in the report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of the fact that you have in such a systematic way presented some reasons for which you consider that the exodus took place of the Albanians, I should like you to hear seven reasons put forward by a prominent German, transmitted by Jurgen Zents [phoen], press representative for the PDS in the German parliament, and then you can tell me whether any of those reasons set forth there you consider to be non-existent or do you consider them to be irrelevant. Here are the seven reasons which he puts forward. But I don't agree with him either because I think the bombing was the prime reason, and he divides this up into seven reasons. But I'd like to hear your views nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll do this systematically. You can put one question at a time rather than a whole series. Now, you can put these points one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness isn't somebody that signs her name with a thumb. She is literate. So I assume she can listen to seven reasons and then tell me after all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The questioning will be proper and it will be in an orderly form. Now, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First, [In English] "People getting killed by NATO's bombings and a desire to escape the general devastation and difficult conditions caused by the aerial assault such as the lack of clean water in nearly all urban areas, electricity, and so on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you talking -- by the way, are you talking about the Kosovo Serb refugees or the Kosovo Albanian refugees in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the refugees, the Albanians. But this refers to both the Albanians and Serbs and all the refugees, Mr. May, because there is no war without refugees. And refugees do -- are not sorted and grouped according to ethnic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll just deal with it in that way. The first -- just a moment. Let the witness answer. The first reason which is apparently given -- let the witness deal with the matter. The first matter which is being put for the refugees is people being killed by NATO bombs, a desire to escape the devastation and difficult conditions. Now, was that a reason that, in your experience and as a result of your findings, which was given by refugees for their leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Fear of getting caught in the crossfire between KLA and Yugoslav military."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you hear that as a reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that that was a significant reason for the departure of the refugees. It was a reason that some people mentioned, particularly those in the rural areas and around what had been very strong KLA areas, Decani, Srbica, these types of areas. So it became a little more geographically related, this particular reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Attacks by Yugoslav soldiers and Serbian police and paramilitary often triggered by KLA attacks carried out under cover of ethnic Albanian civilians."

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this has very little bearing to do with why people left during the air campaign. And by that period, I would say from March 24th onward. Now, prior to that - and this is also covered in the report - there were some incidents inside Kosovo when we were there where attacks in some of the civilian areas did create a smaller displacement of the population. And again, by this, I would refer to the winter exercises in Vucitrn and down in Kacanik as well. But particularly Kacanik is where we did have some KLA and skirmishes with the Yugoslav soldiers that did result in a displacement. Not during the air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Spreading of panic and horror stories in the broadcasts of dozen of small KLA, NATO, or Albanian short-wave radio stations alongside the propaganda broadcast of the KLA from Albania over Radio Tirana."

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monitoring of the media was something that the OSCE did as one of these other ancillary duties I referred to before. I don't recall that the Albanian media contributed in any type of a negligent way to the exodus of the population. We had greater concerns at the time with the media in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can believe that. Next: [In English] "Pillaging bands of Albanian Mafia and KLA who extorted money, looted houses for anything of value, then burned the houses to create the political effect."

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not at all relevant to the periods before and during the air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "KLA troops who declared a general mobilisation, forcing every available man into their military service. Those objecting were subjected to great physical abuse and released only upon paying ransom."

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any allegations with this type of severity. There had been some discussions and some reports in the early days of the refugee crisis in the beginning of April in the Kukes area where you had about 3 or 400 thousand refugees that there was mobilisation that may have been going on in the camps. We looked into it right away from a refugee protection standpoint and did not find it to be any type of organised or systematic way, so we were not aware of any type of forced recruitment by the KLA. And I would just add that it's very common in any type of conflict that I've ever worked in for there always to be these rumours of mobilisation in refugee camps. So that was not out of the ordinary. But we found no evidence to substantiate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you know, because this was when your mission was in Kosovo, that the KLA proclaimed a general mobilisation, made that decision? And we had documents here. This was documented in court that general mobilisation had been proclaimed. Is that something you knew about?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen the mobilisation documents that you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the seventh reason: [In English] "KLA announcements that NATO was about to carry out a massive ground attack." [Interpretation] So of all these seven reasons which he sets out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, if the KLA made such an announcement, it wasn't the reason that the people left Kosovo. The people left Kosovo because they were being terrorised by Yugoslav and Serb security forces, not because any announcements of the nature that you've just put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did anybody mention that as a reason for leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And does it seem to you be logical -- because you say that you only interviewed a handful of Serbs, does it seem to you to be logical that the reasons that you put forward, 100.000 Serb civilians should have left Kosovo during the bombing if the bombing was not a reason?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: While it's true that we only were able to speak with a few Kosovo Serbs for the first report, the second report, which covers the period from June to October 1999, deals extensively with the treatment of the Kosovo Serbs that stayed in Kosovo. As far as the reasons that they left when they reported that they were leaving because they feared NATO bombings, I'm sure that they in fact did fear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, according to what we can deduce as a conclusion from what you said, it was only the Serbs who were afraid of NATO bombing, whereas the Albanians were not afraid of NATO bombing. Is that it? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could make that -- that type of a statement in my capacity as trying to describe what the findings were that we had because we did not have access to the Kosovo Serb refugees during the air campaign. We had access to the Kosovo Serbs that remained in Kosovo after the war, and as I said, their situation is extensively documented in part II of the report, and it is not a pretty picture either. But as far as the reasons why the Serbs left Kosovo during the NATO air campaign, I would have to refer you to other human rights organisations that had access and documented that at the time. It's just not covered in our reports, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've had three-quarters of an hour. This is a more extensive witness; you can have until the break, which will be a total of an hour and a half with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right, then, but I would like to ask the witness to give brief answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Within the second stage of the work, when the mission had withdrawn on the 20th of March, 1999, you said that the department for human rights continued its work in refugee camps in Macedonia and Albania; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you had collected 1.000 statements; right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the total is closer to 2.800, 1.100 of which were collected in the camps from Albania and the remaining in the camps in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me read you your own statement. Let us just ascertain a few facts. At point 11 of your statement: "After its withdrawal from Kosovo, the OSCE-KVM continued to gather information and monitor the human rights situation in Kosovo," et cetera, et cetera. "I supervised and tasked more than 200 staff deployed to refugee camps throughout Albania and Macedonia to collect information. OSCE often set up tents in the camps to provide a private and safe place for speaking to refugees. When this was not possible, OSCE vehicles were used as mobile offices." Therefore, you had 200 staff members. You worked round the clock, day and night, as far as I'm able to understand, and you even used OSCE vehicles as mobile offices. And it emerges from all this that when the number of these 2.000-odd 600 or 764 persons in Macedonia and Albania, which means 2.700 and something, and when you divide that with the number of people you had and the 78 days that there were, it would appear that, per staff member, every person would have needed six and a half days or six days to obtain one statement. Does that indicate an effort to have selectiveness, to obtain data in a selective way which was targeted in your research or not? Were you selective?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you follow the mathematics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do indeed. There's a few factors missing from the conclusion which makes the conclusion wrong. While we had, at full strength, 200 staff members dispersed in Albania and in Macedonia - that included our national colleagues, interpreters, et cetera - seventy-five of those staff were deployed in Albania, which was under a horrendous humanitarian catastrophe because of the influx of so many refugees that came in what seemed to be very controlled spurts of 50.000 a day for a few days, et cetera. So the 200 working a day is a little deceptive. The mission was going through a phase-down at the time, so it took a little while to get organised. So your math is wrong in the way you analyse it. That being said, we were indeed very selective in the information that was coming --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Ms. Mitchell. It's not lose time with all these explanations. It will take up too much time. Let's put that to one side for now. But it is not being contested that the total figure of 2.764, of the total statements taken, was the number. You're not challenging the number of 2.764 statements taken during that period of time; right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer, I apologise. Could you say it again?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that the figure of 800.000 refugees is mentioned? That is the figure that is being used. And what you have of a total of 2.764 individuals, that this is used to confirm some sort of general conclusion as to a figure of 800.000 refugees. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not it. What this report describes is the findings of the 2.764 and draws from that certain conclusions, one of which, based on the fact that we had very much of a representative -- refugees representing all different geographical areas, different age groups, gender, et cetera - we were trying to be very diverse in the way in which we collected the information - that that is a good sampling, we believe, of events that went on in those communities, although we don't have the statements from the other 800.000 refugees. But, no, this report only describes the findings of the 2.764, but there are broader conclusions that are made based on those findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this, but briefly, please: What method did you select your interlocutors? Was it a random sample or did you have some selective method that you used?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of those 2.764.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to be brief. The OSCE/KVM had a very special relationship with the Albanians. We drove around in these very bright orange cars. The Albanian community is a traditional community with the patriarch sort of taking the lead, so what would happen is if we went into a camp, generally the community leaders would approach us, and they may ask for assistance, tell us their needs, et cetera, et cetera, and through that network, we were then able to put out an interest that we were interested in hearing about people's experiences as they left from Kosovo. In particular, we were interested in the more serious crimes and violations that we were hearing about, so witnesses that had been either victims or direct -- directly observed killings, destruction of property, rape, these types of -- any of these what we refer to as critical events, we targeted on those particular individuals, and we tried as well to keep -- make sure that we did interview women as well as men, although it's very, very difficult to get women to come forward on crimes that were committed against them in this particular society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And answer me this: In view of the fact that in your statement you said that you ensured vital information and that these -- this vital information be sent to this institution, when was cooperation established between your department of the OSCE mission and this so-called Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first contact with ICTY came during the planning stages of the mission, which would have been in early -- well, would have been in mid-October to early November, and that was at more of an administrative level. Operationally, that began on January 16th, which was the day after the Racak killings when Ambassador Walker asked that ICTY assist in that investigation. And then regularly since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many individuals with whom your people talked to appeared here in the capacity of witnesses? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't looked at the whole list. I do know several of my colleagues have appeared, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your colleagues. I'm talking about the witnesses, the Albanian witnesses who have appeared.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not looked at that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For your work, as far as I was able to understand from your statement, you were directly responsible to the Head of Mission; right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how frequently did you have meetings with him during your stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that we had meetings only as needed. In the planning stages of the missions, I met with him quite frequently but it was in the context of larger planning discussions. Around specific critical events, I would perhaps meet with him once or twice a day, so that, you know, the days surrounding Racak and some of these other incidents. And then as we withdrew from Kosovo, I started meeting with him more regularly, but always it was in the context of senior staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you do say in your statement that the work of this department of yours reached a peak after the investigation into the killings in Racak. Explain, please, what investigation did you hold with respect to Racak?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Racak happened, it became the responsibility of the Human Rights Division because we had staff with the necessary skill-set to go to the scene, to document it as much as possible with the tools that we had available at that time in the mission. And what we did at Racak was videotape the site, took extensive photographs of the bodies and the injuries to the bodies, took statements from anybody that we could that was a witness or that may have known something about it. We also spoke to the authorities. I myself was dealing with the -- on the forensic side, trying to key up access to the autopsies, things of this nature. We also spoke with the investigating judge and with the police chiefs around the area. The role that I played was to manage that on an operational basis, and by that, I mean following up every day with the witnesses, collecting that information, handling it, liaising with ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you, in the same way as you did in Racak, document other events that you collected information about?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you closely cooperate with Mr. Walker on the matter of Racak?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I closely kept -- I kept Ambassador Walker closely advised of the facts as they were developing, although he did not have access to the statements that were taken. So he would -- didn't read the statements. He received oral summaries from myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you conducted an investigation into the affair, tell me how you came to learn of the events in Racak. Who informed you about it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. When did you receive the first information about Racak? Just be as precise and specific as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first heard about something the evening before, and that was I heard some radio traffic between General Maisonneuve and headquarters. They were transporting people to the hospital. And then there wasn't a lot of news that night. Around -- very early the next morning, prior to the senior staff meeting, I was informed by the Deputy Head of Mission that there had been a situation in Racak that was developing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was in the morning on that day after the events in Racak; right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Walker informed you about that before he went to Racak?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, I think, one of the deputy heads of mission who informed me of it. I did not see Ambassador Walker prior to him going to Racak although I was in touch with others that were travelling with him. My role was to manage things at the headquarters level and deal with all of the inquiries that were coming in as well as put in place what we were going to do the next day and thereafter with regards to this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he inform you of, this assistant of his?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As best as I recall, that there were a lot of bodies at Racak, and the initial numbers were, I think, 12 or 15. And then it went up within 20 minutes to another ten being discovered. So that was an incident on a scale that we had not yet seen in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since that morning, before Walker left to Racak, you were informed about this large number of killed persons. How do you explain the fact that Walker was astonished and surprised when he came there after you had already been informed about this?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing like seeing a sight of so many bodies killed in that manner. That is, I think, shocking to anyone's conscience regardless of whether or not you knew that they would be there. And I don't know why. You'd have to ask Ambassador Walker what he knew. I was dealing with things on the operational level and I was one of the people who had to get folks to the scene so I wasn't too concerned at the time as to what the ambassador's view -- how he was viewing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I assume that what his associate said to you was something that he must have known about too; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's for Ambassador Walker, not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Ian Hendrie work for you?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You informed Ian Hendrie about the events in Racak; right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you sent him there to go there to take photographs?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent him there to document whatever it was that was going on. We were still getting -- all of this was unwinding, and it was all being done by two-way radio, with a lot of people between the radio room and my office in between, so these were events, fast-moving events, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. I understand that, Ms. Mitchell. He claims that you told him that there were very many casualties in Racak, and you say now that one of Walker's assistants informed you about that that morning. What is the name of this assistant of Walker's who informed you about this large number of casualties in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Deputy Head of Mission for the human dimension aspects, which was a German diplomat by the name of Berndt Bouckaert. I worked very closely with Mr. Bouckaert. He would have been in the executive meeting with the Ambassador, came out of that, told me, and then I would have informed Ian to prepare to get out there and take what he needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this meeting held? At what time in the morning when Ian Hendrie managed to get to Racak by noon after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really sure. It would have been anywhere from, I don't know, 8.30 to 10.00. It could have been earlier. I'm afraid I can't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you first come to Racak?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to Racak for several days after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In respect of your investigation, you mentioned the police. Did you have any cooperation with the official investigation authorities of Yugoslavia, with the investigating judge, with the authorities that are officially in charge of carrying out the investigation, the judicial authorities?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received no cooperation from them as far as the sharing of information goes. They would generally indulge us in a meeting, but there was no cooperation or sharing of information on their behalf, although we did provide the forensic institute and the authorities with copies of the pictures that we had taken because they were not there to document the site itself. If anything, I say that the authorities were quite obstructive with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know how many members of the KLA lost their lives in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe after, a few days afterwards, I was provided with a list of seven or nine names of KLA that apparently had lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the report of the Verification Mission of the OSCE for the 16th of January, there was already information about a number of members of the KLA who had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not sure of the exact timing of when I knew some of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A few days later, you say that you went to Racak. And who did you see there as far as the Albanians were concerned? Racak, was it under KLA control then?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The village was pretty much empty still at that point, and I was there not to interview or have any official meetings. I was there more or less just to see the site, to see where we were on the collection of information, what needed to be, you know, looked at again, this type of thing. So my reasons for the visit were not to meet with the local population at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not encounter any locals then, especially not members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any. There were some people in their houses, but again, I was not seeking anyone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, you say that the OSCE staff, before withdrawing from Kosovo, destroyed the documentation that the department had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Destroyed some of the documentation that the department had. We took out all of the active files as well as any other documents that we were concerned about maintaining the security of, that had names of people that had filed human rights allegations, things of this nature. But a vast majority of the documentation was destroyed. A lot of that would have been mission manuals, resource materials, things of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Information related to the events in Racak you submitted to the office of this institution in Skopje, if I understood it correctly. I'm interested in the following: Why didn't you keep copies of the materials related to Racak that you submitted to the office in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not feel that we had adequate enough security in the mission to secure any of the witness statements, and we felt that it would be jeopardising our staff too much if they had statements on their body or in their notebook and were subsequently detained for any reason by the authorities. To have that type of information could have exposed them and put them at risk. These decisions were taken at a time when Ambassador Walker was declared persona non grata. The mission was in a high, high level of security threat and was moving up in preparations for a potential withdrawal. So it was simply a very insecure environment, and we did not want to retain any copies of anything that could have jeopardised a witness in the Racak case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, why did Racak and your work related to Racak have to be exempted from regular procedure?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we had never seen anything of the scale of Racak and our procedures, quite frankly, at that time in the mission were not developed enough to have secured areas, limited access, locked cabinets, these types of things. Everything the mission had, we had to import in from Europe, and we just didn't have these types of resources. So I would say that Racak, to use your words, was exempted from regular procedure because it was a very, very shocking and irregular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously your contribution to the creation of this indictment for Kosovo was a major one. Did you cooperate in that direction with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a comment by you for which there is no justification. Now, what is your question of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Fred Abrahams from Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have good cooperation with him as well during the work that you've been referring to, these questions that we've been dealing with just now?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen Fred a few times over the years in the field. We've kept in touch by e-mail, but we were professional colleagues. He had -- not despite his -- his interest was not consulted with directly for the preparation of any of these reports. He was working on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can one infer, regardless of the fact that he worked independently and did not work on this, that he worked on the parallel project of the Human Rights Watch, a book that is entitled "Under Orders"? Was there any cooperation between you and him, and to what extent, and the teams that were working on both books?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing formal between OSCE and Human Rights Watch. We went through great efforts because of the nature of the OSCE. It is not a non-governmental organisation. It is, in fact, the other creature. So we worked very hard not to share information with our colleagues. We did not share interview -- interview forms, leads, or anything like this. What we did share with NGOs, I think it was in the middle of May, was the form that we were using to collect the information, which is attached to my addendum - and that was a standardised interviewing form - and the framework for a database to index the type of information. But I really don't know if anybody ever used it. It was available. But we did not collaborate with Human Rights Watch at all, although we spoke and discussed our ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us leave that subject now. Until the mission withdrew, about 1.400 verifiers were in a position to talk to everybody on the spot, in the field, and to check out assertions or objections on the various spots. That was the situation until the 20th of March; right? After the 20th of March, you received information from Albanian sources only. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's incorrect, the first part of your sentence, that we had 1.400 verifiers in a position to talk to everybody on the spot. We had restricted freedom of movement the entire time that we were in Kosovo. It was very difficult to have private conversations in detention areas. So we did not -- we were not in a position to talk to anybody anywhere, ever. You are correct that after our withdrawal from Kosovo, our access to Kosovo Serbs was greatly restricted by events and we primarily were speaking to Albanian refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as for the information that you were now receiving only from one side, so any kind of balance that might have been there, a balance of objectivity, was disrupted. So did you check this out in any valid way?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that the reports were not released until December, there was a long period of analysis. There was ongoing investigations now that were being conducted in Kosovo after the air campaign for the violations committed largely against the minorities and the Kosovo Serbs in particular. So we did have an opportunity to step back after the refugee interviews were collected and analyse the information and take other factors into account; developments on the ground, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. According to the information published on the 5th of March, 1999, in the Albanian newspaper Koha Ditore -- you told us a little while ago that you were following all the media, so then according to the Albanian newspaper Koha Ditore that is being published in Pristina, in the territory of Macedonia at that time, there were 6.000 refugees. So before you give me an answer to this question -- so this is March 1999, just before the campaign. Before you give me an answer to that, I have another question: Are you aware of the statement made by John Saxon, a US congressman, who said that the humanitarian catastrophe in Kosovo started when NATO started its bombing? Do you share that view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer that. That's the view of that particular gentleman. You can call him to give evidence if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I asked the lady, who worked there at the time, and I also referred to a piece of material evidence. This is an Albanian source, stating that there were 6.000 refugees in Macedonia. And also, I quoted a statement of a congressman of hers who said that there was a humanitarian catastrophe in Kosovo when the bombing started. So why would that be wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you can ask is this: Was she aware of the statement which was made in a newspaper on the 5th of March that there were 6.000 refugees -- just a moment. Let me finish. That there were 6.000 refugees in Macedonia then and, from her knowledge, was it correct or not? Can you help us about that, Ms. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of the number of 6.000. I would say that that number seems low to me. There were several hundred thousand refugees still, some of them displaced in Macedonia. I say that because I've subsequently worked in Macedonia, I know the refugee numbers there. From the 1998 conflict, there were some displaced in Macedonia that never returned, and then in March we would have already been experiencing displacement movements in the Kacanik area. So 6.000 may have been a new influx during the period in which Koha Ditore wrote its article, but I think the overall number have been higher at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In attachment 3 to your book entitled "Graveyards," you mention the names of 216 Albanians exhumed at a locality -- at localities that are in 28 Kosovo municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what are you referring to? You're referring to Annex 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Annex 3 to the second volume of your book and it is entitled "Graves Documented by the OSCE." You mentioned the names of 216 Albanians who were exhumed at localities in 28 Kosovo municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't counted up all of the names, but that's correct, Annex 3 is a summary of gravesites that were documented by OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any information about how and in which way these persons had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the procedure was for documenting gravesites was teams would deploy, after coordination with ICTY and others that were doing this task at that time and they would take GPS readings, global positioning readings, sketch out the site, photograph it and then document photograph the exhumation as it was occurring, the clothing, et cetera, and would also gather statements at that time, if appropriate, from family, friends, anybody that may know something about it, and that information would then be shared. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, I'm not asking about your methodology. I'm asking you whether you know how these persons lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't know for any specific one. That's the methodology used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The answer is you don't know. You do not know. All right. So you do not know that. And you spoke here, for example, about these 216 that you discovered, that your Minister of Defence of the then Clinton administration said, that about 100.000 Albanians of military age were probably killed in Kosovo then. What do you say to this discrepancy between 100.000 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't hear the question, Mr. May, because you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said how do you explain this discrepancy between reality and such statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to deal with what the Minister of Defence said. And your time is almost up, so two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then two questions, and here they come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since FBI experts and Spanish forensic experts carried out investigations after actually dealing with them on site, established that the figures ranged between 187 and 200 persons, do you know that none of these experts, without having carried out their professional work before that, did not say anything about the cause of death before they actually ascertained what had happened and let alone they didn't say anything about the ethnicity of the victims?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since Mr. May gave me the right to put one more question, tell me, do you think that your book and your statistics represent a justification for the NATO aggression and all the horrors it caused not only in Kosovo but throughout Yugoslavia? Does it constitute justification for the crime committed against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the reports document a gross and systematic violation of human rights affecting 90 per cent of the population during a 7.800-day [sic] period committed by the Yugoslav and Serbian security forces. That's what the reports support. And as far as what events happened after that, I don't believe it's addressed in the report or is something I'm really qualified to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try and finish, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I just have one matter. Should I do it right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Does it right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, just one question for you. During the cross-examination, there were various allegations of selectiveness of the report and in the way that you obtained -- the data was obtained, that it was done in a selective way. What would be the response for that from the OSCE and you as director, being directed the work? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, OSCE is comprised of 55 nations. For an organisation to document violations of this scale by, indeed, a member country, required that the highest standards be applied. Also the fact that the OSCE had never released reports of this nature before, so the baseline standards included all of the international treaties and documents that were pre-existing - I think there were 23 in Yugoslavia at the time - as well as the conventions of the Council of Europe, the European Court for Human Rights, et cetera. We tried our best to train the staff so that we would have consistency in the way the information was being collected, to standardise things as much as possible, largely because we were dealing with a mission staff comprised of representatives of the 55 countries, so we had colleagues of varying degrees of English and experience, and English is the working language. So what I would say is that we used incredible care, bearing in mind the gravity of the findings that this report would have for the organisation as a whole, as well as for those accused of the violations. We used -- as we learned to do this process, as it went along, we tried to respond to events as they came up. One particularly, the collection of information regarding rape and sexual abuse, as I said before, a very delicate, difficult topic to deal with in a normal criminal setting let alone in a conflict in the widespread manner in which it happened. So for rape, and this is in the report as well, there were additional procedures that we put in place, trying to make sure that women were the ones doing the interviewing and additional protections given, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's all for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll hear Mr. Hendrie, is that right, after the adjournment? And we will deal with the Rule 70 matters in the final session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I now hear that the next witness is Hendrie, and I have K30 on the list. How come Hendrie now? He's not on the list at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was mentioned yesterday by Mr. Nice that this witness is interposed. The only point about which he's going to give evidence is the suggestion that the bodies in Racak were moved and that the photographs were in some way rigged, a suggestion which you made. His evidence will be limited to that point only. Very well. Twenty minutes. Back at five to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Hendrie, we've asked you to come back to deal with one particular point in your evidence, which you'll hear about in a moment. You are under the declaration which you've already taken, so there's no need for you to take it again. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is the point? We need to get on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an objection. I didn't want to waste time on it during the cross-examination because it didn't have anything to do with the previous witness, but with you, Mr. May. You said that during my cross-examination of the previous witness that I misrepresented the facts and distorted the facts with respect to Racak. Now, I'm asking you, does this mean that you are pre-empting your decision with respect to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, of course not. It was a comment on the question that you were asking, and you pointed out that the question you were asking was to do with Rogovo. So the matter is over. And since it related to Rogovo, you were entitled to make the point. As far as Racak is concerned, it's very much an issue, and that is what this witness is going to deal with. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld, are you going to deal with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I should say that you can cross-examine the witness, Mr. Milosevic, this witness, but only on those matters which are subject of evidence in chief by the Prosecution. You can then cross-examine. Your time will be limited to the same as that taken by the Prosecution. So it's on a very limited issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, you will recall giving evidence before this Court last day. I can tell you that after you had been excused, another witness was shown copies of your photographs taken and contained at tab 5 of the Racak 1 binder. Ambassador Walker was referred to some of your photographs and asked questions about those photographs. In particular, my recollection is that photographs marked in these proceedings under ERN number 732354 and 732355 were referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you show this to the witness and put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, looking at it, do you recognise those photographs as being among the photographs you took on the 16th of January, 1999, at Racak?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, sir, it has been suggested that there is a difference in those photographs in that one photograph seems to show blood and the other does not. Can you just look at those photographs for a moment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's also been suggested that the presence of blood in one photograph and the apparent absence of blood in the other indicates that the scene has been staged or rigged. I'm going to ask you, sir, what is the time interval between -- approximate time interval between the taking of these photographs? Were they taken at about the same time?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: One or two minutes at most, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So if the allegation of staging or rigging, it would have had to have been during your presence, then, I take it.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, have you, since taking these photographs, had an opportunity to look at the computer-generated image of the entire negatives of the camera that you had at that time on the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And are you, from the number, the sequential numbers of those photographs, able to determine in which order they were taken?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Before I show you the computer-generated images, I'm also going to ask the usher to show you what has been marked, it's the next page in the binder, 732356. Is that also a photograph of the same individual, and is that one of the photographs that you took on the date in question?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I would now ask you to show the witness three photographs, computer-generated, with the sequential numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm showing you that first photograph. On the roll of photographs that you took, are you able to determine what number that one was?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Of the sequence at this particular scene of this body, it's the first one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And does it have a number at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Could you look at the next photograph in the sequence, number 12, if you would. Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: This is photograph number 732356 in the bundle, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And that was number 12. And there appears to be a hand -- can you describe what is depicted in that photograph and if you know whose hand that is?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's mine, Your Honour. It's showing me examining the rear of the -- of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what did you note underneath the body and the rear of the body?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Blood, Your Honour, as you can see on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The next photograph, please. That would be the third one in the sequence of these three, would it, number 13?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And now we see -- what can -- you see the presence of blood in this photograph now?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, you can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court, if you would, please, if you are able, what you saw on that day and how it is that these photographs depict blood in one and apparently not in the other?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's explained for two reasons, Your Honour. The first one is the camera angle is different from the first and third photographs, and the other element is my looking or examining the rear of the body. The first photograph, Your Honour, number 11, is taken at a different angle and at a lower angle, so the blood is actually concealed by -- by the body. If you examine number 13, Your Honour, you can clearly see blood and a hand-sized rock which are concealed by the head and shoulder of the deceased in photograph number 11. I would like to add, Your Honour, that at no time did I see anyone placing blood or anything of that nature near, at any time, at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, has the hat been moved? It appears from the photographs that it is in a different location in relation to the body. Are you able to explain if -- first of all, from your own recollection, whether or not the hat was moved while you were taking these photographs?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't recall the hat being moved or being moved by me. If you examine photograph number 13 and 11 and at the peak of the hat there's a rock which is embedded into the soil, and that's in the same relative position to the hat in both photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There's also a shadow of a sort of an object that points in the direction of the hat, and there are some rocks visible. Are you able to determine from that whether or not the hat appears to be in the same position or in a different position?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: From the position of the rocks and the shadows, the hat is in the same position, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, it's clear from the sequence that you have produced to us that you lifted the head of the body between number 11 and 13; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you lifted the body, did you note any blood underneath the head in the location that is now shown in photograph 13, if we want to call it that? That would be 54 and 55, for the documents before the Court.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: There was blood underneath -- under the shoulders and head of the deceased, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
