utterances.text: All right. Secondly, sir, there were a number of photographs shown to Ambassador Walker, and many of those suggested that there was blood in some photographs and no blood in others. I'm going to ask that you be shown, please, from tab 5, I'm going to show you four photographs from your own set of photographs for one individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For Your Honours, that's numbers -- tab 5, bearing 732362, to 732365. That's a series of four sequential photographs. And I'll just give those to Madam Usher. I wonder, would Your Honours -- I propose to tender the last three photographs, the computer-generated ones with the numbers as exhibits in these proceedings since reference has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 244.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave those for Madam Usher. All right. Do we have a video image?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, if you, just very briefly, look at these photographs, are those photographs at tab 5 of the Racak binder photographs that you took? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are they of the same individual?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from those photographs, is blood visible on all of those photographs?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, sir. On photograph 732363, which is showing a gunshot wound, it's not apparent that there's blood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you look at 362, the first one that's now on the ELMO, is blood visible there?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And on the subsequent photographs, sir, is there blood visible on that individual?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: On the photograph, yes, sir, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now, if I may, three photographs from tab 6, bearing numbers 7639, 7640, and 7641. I hasten to point out these are not photographs taken by you. First of all, do you recognise the scene depicted in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And are you able to determine from just looking at the photograph or snow or ice conditions or shadows or anything whether or not they're approximately the same time as when you took yours? Are you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: It would appear that they were -- the photographs were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put the picture on the ELMO so the accused can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was hoping would happen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, depending on the camera angle, is blood visible in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you put the other two photographs on sequentially as well, please. And the next. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, do the images depicted in those photographs, how do they compare with your recollection of that individual whom you photographed?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's in the same position, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how about the presence or absence of blood?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: The blood is in the same position, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are all my questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to exhibit those particular photographs or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I would, please. I think as a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or are they all in the Racak binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: They're all in the Racak binder, therefore they're before the Court. I just wanted to bring the numbers to the Court's attention so the record would show. The difficulty with the cross-examination of Ambassador Walker is that, although photographs were shown, no reference to numbers were made, and it is only a description in the transcript and recollection of counsel as to which photographs were shown to Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. So the ones that I did want exhibited, you've given numbers to. Those are those three computer-generated images with the sequential numbers 11, 12, and 13. Those are my questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, if you want to ask any questions of this witness about these particular photographs, you can do so. You are alleging that these photographs are rigged. Now is your opportunity to put it to the witness, which you should have done earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the comment to what Mr. Ryneveld said a moment ago that Walker was not told of the photograph numbers, in view of the fact that I was using your photographs in which every photograph had a number, that doesn't stand. That objection doesn't stand. But let's go back to the photograph of the man in the cap with blood, without blood. So may we have both photographs placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm going to ask whether it is clearly visible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have the photographs on the projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: These are the ones that were shown to the witness but there are also the computer-generated ones that are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it clear, looking at this, there is blood or there is no blood on the area between the left side of the head and the cap?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: On the photograph number 354, there is, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also clear that this same space, the space between the left-hand side of the head and the cap, can be seen on the photograph which has one more number and ends in a 5 rather than a 4?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: The area is concealed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Is it then clear that this, in this first photograph, is a pool of blood -- that the pool of blood is in fact above the height of the left ear, almost up on a level on a par with the head by the stone? And is it clear that on this second photograph, on the left-hand side of the head, not up until the top but at any space whatsoever, there is no trace of blood?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: As I've previously explained, Your Honour, there is another photograph in between these two, and it shows that I've actually examined the rear of the deceased and that the photographs are actually taken from different angles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But from every angle we are able to see the space between the left-hand side of the head and the cap. And in the photograph where there is visible blood, there is a lot of blood between the left-hand side Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the head and the cap. You can see blood. On one of the photographs, there is blood. On the other photograph, there's not a trace of blood between the head and the cap. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I repeat the previous answer I've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No need to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't move the cap. That's right; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's my recollection, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that between these two photographs that you were shown, that one minute elapsed in time between one being taken and the other being taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, Your Honour, I said a few minutes, but it was a short period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you didn't move the cap. You didn't make any changes. Only on the soil, the soil, the ground that can be seen on both the photographs, there is blood in one of the photographs and not on the other. Now, the soil and ground between the head and the cap, can you see it, that space, on both the photographs? Is it visible?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you can't see the earth between the head and the cap. On which photograph can you not see the soil; on the one where there is no blood?

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: The area where the blood is is concealed in photograph number 355.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Can you see that the blood is to be found on the level of the upper part of the head, far above the left ear, whereas in the spot where there is no blood, you can see a clear space on the left-hand side above and below the ear and you can see this space between the ear and the cap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've already put this, Mr. Milosevic, and the witness has given his explanation. Now, what is it you're suggesting happened here? If you're suggesting that there has been some sort of foul play, then you should put it clearly to the witness so he can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that it is quite senseless to discuss a fact -- the fact that on one picture, on one photograph, you can see blood and on the other you can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you suggesting he did? He's given his explanation as to how it comes about. You are apparently -- just a moment. You're apparently asserting something else. Now, the witness should have the opportunity of dealing with it. What are you suggesting happened?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I am saying and claiming only what I can see with my own eyes and what you can see with your own eyes. And I claim that this whole situation scene has been rigged, set up, because it is impossible for there to be blood on one spot and no blood in the other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How in this case has it been rigged? What is it you are suggesting has happened?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am claiming that the bodies were brought in from somewhere else and that this whole scenario was rigged and of the alleged place where the execution took place, using photographs of this kind and that it is only through the lack of care on the part of the person who rigged this that these photographs came into our hands. It was a slip that these photographs came to be in our hands too. That is what I am saying, Mr. May, and that is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the slip here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably that they looked through the photographs, the same people who had rigged the alleged massacre in Racak. Because had they been careful, they would not have given us so many photographs on which there was no blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what you're suggesting, are you, is that this witness photographed the body in this case in one place and then photographed it in another? Is that what you're suggesting? So that he can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I am saying that he probably photographed this on that same spot but that the time lapse between the first photograph and the second photograph, in that meantime, somebody spilt some blood or some liquid to make this look like a real scene. And the people who were responsible for that were the people who staged this whole scene and rigged it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Hendrie, who took you there while you were taking these photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, wait a minute. I don't remember that whether the picture which was allegedly taken between these two pictures was shown on the -- was put on the ELMO so that he was able -- Mr. Milosevic and the public gallery was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be done now, if it wasn't before. I believe it was, but -- could we use the computer-generated one, I think it's clearer. The computer-generated ones, Your Honour, sets out the sequence and shows the witness's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's start, if you would, with the first -- Mr. Hendrie, would you help us with the photographs. Let's start with 11, then let's put on 12, and then let's put on 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first photograph, Your Honour, number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second, number 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, that is you, you say, moving the head --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to demonstrate the wound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the final photograph, sir, is number 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how long between those three, would you estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few minutes at most, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So what is suggested, so that we can get this plain, is that while you were photographing, somebody came along with some blood or some other liquid to make it look like blood and splashed it around. Now, did anything like that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, how do you explain this, Mr. Hendrie: How do you explain the origin of the blood on the soil where there had been no blood when the first photograph was taken? Because the interim photograph shows the right-hand side. That is not brought into question at all. Why is there no blood on the first photograph between the cap and the left-hand side? It could not have been invisible in this photograph 55.

utterances.speaker: IAN ROBERT HENDRIE [Recalled]
utterances.text: Sir, I've already explained that. The photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you better explain it. It appears the accused doesn't understand or will not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, this is the first photograph that I took. It's clear from the angle that there's no blood visible next to the body. The second photograph that I took shows me lifting the head of the deceased, showing an injury and blood on the clothing and his head. The third and final photograph I took shows a patch of blood by the left shoulder of the deceased. It's clear from this photograph, comparing it to the first photograph, that the angle that the photograph was taken was different. If you look at the shadows, there's very little difference, if any, of the length of shadow, which would indicate that the photographs were taken very -- within a very short time space. If you examine the photograph near the white hat, the rocks which are embedded into the soil appear in the same relative position to the hat in both the first and third photograph. This is the first photograph, and the -- just above and slightly to the left of the hat is a rock, a linear rock, which appears to be embedded in the soil. On the final photograph, number 13, you see a greater area of rock, and the rocks and the hat appear to be in the same or relative position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, if you want to ask some questions about that or anything more, your time is limited. We'll give you five extra minutes to ask some more questions, if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have several questions for Mr. Hendrie, apart from this one photograph, because Mr. Ryneveld showed only one photograph of a corpse without blood and I showed at least ten photographs here, about ten. So he did not comment upon those ten-odd photographs at all where there had also been no blood. But let's complete this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that the photograph that ends with number 55 was taken from a certain angle so that it is lower in terms of the position of the head and the position of the body and the photograph that was positioned was put above? So in both cases this difference that is very slight, this difference makes it possible to see exactly the same terrain, the exact same piece of soil between the left ear and the cap. Is it clear that there is a bloodstain between the left ear and the cap on number 54 and on number 55 there is nothing between the left ear and the cap? Draw a straight line between the left ear and the cap, from that place where one would put glasses, for example, and then you will see that there is nothing on photograph 55. So is there any doubt about that, that this is the same soil? And the witness claims that he did not move the corpse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has already dealt with this point. You've put it several times in various forms. Mr. Hendrie, is there anything you want to add to what you've already said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe we've covered it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please, Mr. Hendrie, could you give me an answer to a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you finished with this photographs? Have we finished with this sequence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems that you want to explain to me that I cannot see with my very own eyes that there is blood on one photograph and there is no blood on the other photograph and that it's on the same soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the photographs be brought back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that the scene had been rigged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got any other questions for this witness or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, on that morning, when did Sandra Mitchell inform you that you were supposed to go to Racak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to go into that. Your cross-examination is limited to the matters which he raised this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Please. Since you're a police officer, do you know -- let me ask this: Do you know that witnesses, alleged witnesses of this event, claim that these people were shot at from the hill towards the ravine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not what he gave evidence about this morning. I'm going to bring this examination to a close. Mr. Wladimiroff, have you any questions you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to ask him, Mr. May. I want to ask him about this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He's not given evidence about that. I told you at the outset the cross-examination is limited because this witness has already come here once to give evidence and been cross-examined at some length by you. This is purely limited to the matters which he gave evidence about. Mr. Ryneveld, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: None, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendrie, thank you for coming back to the Tribunal. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution will call Mr. Shukri Aliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I should mention something while we're waiting for the witness. We've had information that the case which was going to sit in this court next week in the afternoons is no longer going to do so, so we have the afternoons available, which we propose to take up. In fact, it will mean simply this: That we will be able to sit on Monday afternoon in this case. Tuesday afternoon we're already engaged in another case, and likewise on Wednesday. It means we won't have to interrupt this case for the provisional release, so we'll have the entire morning available and perhaps some more time, depending on how the day and week goes, but we will have Monday afternoon available. Perhaps you could take that into your consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We will certainly factor that into our plans, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might just address you on that very point while we're waiting for the witness. Ambassador Vollebaek is scheduled for Monday, and in the event we do not complete this witness that we're about to start today, might we perhaps wrap him around Vollebaek, if necessary, because Ambassador Vollebaek has restricted time availability. That's my only request at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll consider how far we get this morning. Yes. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would put the earphones on. If you would take the declaration. Perhaps the usher could hand the witness the declaration so he can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your full name --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your full name and spell your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: No. Yes, I can hear you now. The thing's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let's try again. Sir, can you please state your full name and spell your last name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Shukri A-l-i-u.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of May, 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Ryt [phoen] in the municipality of Dragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, are you of Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I'm of Albanian ethnicity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 1971, did you join the army of Yugoslavia, then known as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. In 1971, I was -- I became an officer in the Yugoslav army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you eventually obtain the rank of captain first class?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I reached the rank of captain first class in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From 1974 to 1979, what was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: From 1974 to 1979, I commanded a unit of reserve officers in Prizren for firing, specialty firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And from 1980 to 1987, what was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1987, I was in -- at the headquarters of Kosova Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that headquarters located in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. The headquarters of the Kosova Territorial Defence was located in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we'll go a little bit more quickly if, whenever possible, you answer a yes-or-no question just with yes or no. When you were assigned to the Territorial Defence headquarters in Pristina, what were your duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: My duty was to work with the Territorial Defence headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what specific --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: -- and exercises in specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of exercises?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Exercises with the units of Territorial Defence, such as exercising units working with weapons and firing skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point during your career, did you complete university studies?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I finished my studies in Belgrade at the faculty of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you finish your studies by correspondence or were you living in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I finished my studies in correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the curriculum that you undertook at the faculty of defence in Belgrade? What courses did you take?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: It was a four-year programme at the faculty. All subjects. Mostly military subjects: Command structures, leadership, biological and chemical weapons, tactics, strategy, and other fields, and liaison work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you obtain a degree, and if so, in what year?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. In 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after you obtained your first degree in military studies did you perform any post-graduate studies?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I was at the defence university at -- defence faculty at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. university in Belgrade, but for personal reasons I couldn't finish my studies, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During your time as a JNA officer and as a result of your professional education, did you become therefor familiar with the structure and operations of the JNA that subsequently became the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you become --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I became familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you become familiar with the principles of command?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to turn your mind, please, to 1987, Mr. Aliu. In that year 1987, were you accused of providing firearms to Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: In 1987, I was accused, and I was convicted of three months -- sentenced to three months' probation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was this charge true or false?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The charge was not true. It was a falsification. I was framed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after that, did you remain in the army?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: No. I was not able to continue my work at the headquarters and was forced to -- I was transferred to the provincial defence secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was your position at the provincial defence secretariat?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: In the provincial defence secretariat, I worked as a counsellor in the Civilian Protection Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about the structure and the work of this secretariat. Briefly, what was the tasks or the responsibilities of the provincial defence secretariat for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The provincial defence secretariat in Kosova was an administrative organ which primarily supplied -- provided support and logistic support for mobilisation and support for the so-called Kosovo Corps, which was the main form in Kosova, support for the secretary of the interior, and liaison activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear and everyone understands, this Kosovo Corps that you refer to -- that you referred to, was this a corps of the VJ army or what was then the JNA army but that which became part of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The Kosovo Corps was a constituent part of the 3rd Army of Nis consisting of seven brigades, and was entirely mobilised in 1998 for military operations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that in a minute. Just structurally --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- would it be fair to think, then, of the Kosovo Corps and the secretariat where you worked as two separate but parallel organisational structures?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The corps and the secretariat were two separate organisations, but they were together for coordination purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And in 1994 and 1995, who became the chief of the secretariat for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: In 1994, 1995, the chief of the secretariat was Petar Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so at that time, then, did Petar Ilic become your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. He was my supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the years that Petar Ilic was your supervisor, Mr. Aliu, did you become familiar with his signature?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I would know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Petar Ilic sign his name in Latin script or in Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: After 1990, Cyrillic was used, especially after the abolition of the Kosova constitution, and Petar Ilic always signed in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to be clear again, was the Civilian Protection Unit where you worked part of the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In time of crisis or war, what was the task of the Civilian Protection Unit?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: As the protection secretariat, generally operated in drawing up and mobilising plans, and especially in making up, reinforcing the units of the corps and the Secretariat for the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, when you say "reinforcing the units of the corps," do you mean in a classic military fighting sense or do you mean providing some other kind of assistance?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: It wasn't -- it was more a matter of reinforcements for the conduction of operations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And what kind of work or tasks would the Civilian Protection Unit be assigned to do?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Making up with conscripts the units of the corps, making up with conscripts the police, and making up the civilian defence units in the provincial defence secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. We may get into a problem now with translation because it's my understanding that the word "protection" and "defence" are the same in Albanian, but I'm going to ask you this question and I hope we can make this clear. Apart from the unit called the Civilian Protection Unit, was there also an entity called Defence Civilian Units or Civilian Defence units?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: In 1987, all the Territorial Defence was disarmed. I will explain this, if you will allow me. With the disarming of the Territorial Defence and the abolition of the constitution in 1989 and the speech that the accused made in Fushe Kosova, all the weapons of the Territorial Defence went over to civil protection units, and for this, the military district was responsible, and it was the provincial defence secretariat that was responsible for conscripts. If you will allow me, I will continue for just a minute, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me try to make this a little bit clearer, if I can.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You worked for a unit called the Civilian Protection Unit. What was the difference between the Civilian Protection Unit where you worked and the Defence Civilian Unit where other people worked?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The Civilian Protection Units had the main task of helping the population in the case of various perils, whereas the Defence Civilian Units, which were forbidden to carry arms under the Geneva Conventions, replaced the Civilian Defence Units of the former Territorial Defence units, and they were now called Defence Civilian Units and were mainly made up of Serbian citizens, and not a single Albanian was included in them after the late 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But after the late 1980s, were these Defence Civilian Units armed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, they were all armed with all the arsenal that was taken from the Territorial Defence units or, rather, looted from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The Defence Civilian Units were armed with these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. During the spring of 1998, did you become aware of a new military organ that was formed in Pristina? Just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: During 1998, the staff was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was this staff or organ called?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: This might be called a joint staff or, rather, a war staff of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you personally participate in meetings of this joint staff or the war staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: No. These were secret meetings, and I wouldn't dare to take part in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, how did you obtain information about this joint staff that was set up in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: After the corps command was in the centre of Prishtina, that is the provincial secretariat and the command in the same building, I received information from conversations that took place in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was there a particular person who you knew who was a member of this joint command?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: There were many that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you name one of them, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, let me -- let's go a little bit more slowly. Did any of your colleagues participate in this joint staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: In this staff, in this joint staff which led our operations in Kosova, there was Milomir Minic, the chairman of the political and social chamber of Yugoslavia; Nikola Sainovic, the Deputy Prime Minister; Zoran Andjelkovic, whom the accused delegated to be head of the Kosova government; Veljko Odalovic, the head of Prishtina district; Vojo Zivkovic, chairman of the Serbian Socialist Party; his deputy, Mitar Samardzic; General Nebojsa Pavkovic; General Lazarevic; Petar Ilic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is this the same Petar Ilic who was the --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: -- Misko Lakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is this the same Petar Ilic who was the head of the secretariat and your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, the same Petar Ilic. Misko Lakovic, the head of state security of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this joint staff with Petar Ilic?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I didn't discuss the work of this -- I didn't discuss the work of this staff with Petar Ilic but I did mention its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Petar Ilic mentioned this existence -- mentioned the existence of the joint staff to you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he mentioned -- he mentioned it several times at the secretariat. And he took part at all the meetings of the staff that took place at 5.00 in the afternoon every Tuesday, depending on the situation in Kosova. And Nikola Sainovic often came to the military command of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where did these meetings occur, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: These meetings mainly were held in the Kosova parliament, in Andjelkovic's office, and sometimes in the former provincial committee, and according to circumstances, at the military command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on occasion did you ever see the members of this joint staff arrive for these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I often saw Nikola Sainovic arriving at the command of the Prishtina Corps, and also General Lazarevic, as commander of the corps, also often arrived at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was your belief and understanding regarding the tasks of this joint staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The duties of the staff could be interpreted very easily, because all the units of the Prishtina Corps were ready for war. They were mobilised. And also the internal affairs units and also the Civilian Defence units were also armed, even though this is strictly forbidden under the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't think you've quite answered my question. My question was: What was your belief and understanding regarding the work or the tasks of this joint staff? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Specifically, I believe that this staff planned military operations in Kosova. It planned armed conflicts. This joint staff was really involved in operational matters and drawing up plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, since you did not participate in any of the meetings of this joint staff, what was the basis for your belief about the work of this joint staff or joint command?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: On the basis of my own work at the secretariat and information that reached the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there other joint staffs or joint commands set up at the municipal level in Kosovo around this time?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: On the basis of this joint staff, in all the municipalities of Kosova there were staffs, war staffs, formed, generally headed by the chairmen of the municipalities and who led the municipal staffs. There was 28 of them in all at municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the chief task of these municipal staffs?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The main task of these municipal staffs was to prepare for war and to conduct the war in Kosova against the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who was being prepared for war?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: All the units that I mentioned. The Civilian Defence units, the Civilian Protection Units, the Prishtina Corps and the Secretariat for the Interior, but mainly the Serbian population themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, could you tell us the basis of your knowledge of these? You said earlier that your basis is your own work at the secretariat and information that reached the secretariat. Could you be more specific? How did you know about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in the Territorial Defence staff for eight years at the time when it consisted of Albanians and Serbs together. Normally a certain percentage were Albanians. But after the disarming of the Territorial Defence in 1987 and the abolition of the constitution in 1989, the Albanians were expelled from all their jobs and especially in the Territorial Defence where these Civilian Protection Units were formed. And in the civilian defence units, there was not a single Albanian, and they consisted solely of members of the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, I'm asking about the joint command that you mentioned. You said it was the organ that was preparing war against Kosovo Albanians. What was your base of that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This staff was formed by the accused, and this staff throughout -- operated throughout the war in Kosova down to 1999, and you can see what happened in the streets and cities of Kosova and throughout the territory of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Saxon can assist us with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, can you describe any specific information that reached your ears during 1998 or the first part of 1999 that described the work and the activities of this joint staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: I didn't receive any specific information in writing because this information was secret and went only to specific places such as the army command. But by looking at how they behaved in Kosova, you could see how they were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you receive any verbal information as to what the members of this joint command were doing?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Verbal information, we received this in the provincial secretariat from Petar Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please tell the Judges specifically of the kind or kinds of verbal information that Petar Ilic passed to you regarding the work of the joint staff.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: The joint staff had the main task of leading policy in Kosova and Serbian ideology, promoting Serbian ideology, and to give total support to the command of the Prishtina Corps and the Secretariat for the Interior in fulfilling their military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, can you read Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you some documents, then, and I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Saxon, if you're coming -- if you're coming to a different area of the evidence, it might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, we're going to have to adjourn the evidence now until Monday morning. I'm sorry you are being kept over, but we have to deal with another matter now. Could you be back, please, at 9.00 on Monday morning, and could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of July, 2002, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25
